data.title: Middle East Eye: US-Israeli former soldier on visit to Netherlands accused of Gaza war crimes
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
US-Israeli former soldier on visit to Netherlands accused of Gaza war crimes
The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint in the Netherlands against a former US-Israeli soldier accused of involvement in attacks on schools sheltering displaced Palestinians, mass detentions and the destruction of residential buildings in Gaza.
The complaint, submitted to the Dutch National Public Prosecutor's Office on 4 November, names Noam Himmelman, a former member of the Israeli army's Netzah Yehuda Battalion, who is currently in Amsterdam.
HRF alleges that Himmelman was involved in war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide during Israel's war on Gaza. The complaint was filed under the Dutch International Crimes Act, which allows prosecution of international crimes when suspects are present on Dutch territory.
According to HRF, Israeli forces, including the battalion, surrounded schools in Beit Hanoun on 16 April 2024, where thousands of displaced Palestinians had sought shelter. Soldiers allegedly fired on the school complex and detained dozens of men, including elderly people and teenagers, forcing them to strip before taking them away.
HRF says Himmelman documented the arrests in an Instagram story that it subsequently verified and geolocated to a military outpost near the school.
The foundation also alleges that between January and July 2025, the battalion conducted controlled demolitions of residential buildings across Beit Hanoun, contributing to the extensive destruction of the town. Himmelman served with the unit during these operations.
The complaint cites the battalion's previous record of alleged abuses, including the 2022 death of 78-year-old Palestinian-American Omar Assad after he was detained by its soldiers.

For years, mainstream media has been criticised for its failure to report accurately on Israel’s genocide in Gaza, allowing Israel to commit crimes with impunity.
In July the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, Fransesca Albanese, released a report about the media complicity in genocide.
Her report details how the systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists, Israeli media’s incitement, and the legitimisation from international coverage have facilitated genocide and obstructed accountability.
Outlets relied heavily on Israeli sources, using the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 to justify Israel’s subsequent onslaught and present the conflict as though it began exclusively with the attack.
It was frustration with this narrative that prompted Maria Robles, an independent researcher and artist, to begin research into archival American newspaper stories.
She wanted to “share the reality” of what was happening in Palestine through “public history and public memory - not based on opinion, but aggregating existing materials, existing research, existing journalism and making it as accessible as possible to the public”.
Over three years, Robles collated more than 3,000 clippings from almost 700 papers dating from 1724 to 2023, using online archives and physical records, and in doing so, establishing Covering Palestine.
Robles had previously worked on a research campaign to raise awareness about the history of slavery in New York using publicly available archive material.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump claims 'minor strikes' on Iran's Qeshm Island, but says talks ongoing
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Trump claims 'minor strikes' on Iran's Qeshm Island, but says talks ongoing
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/07/2026 - 09:13
The claimed attack comes shortly after Trump's Republican Party suffered a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections
US President Donald Trump speaks during NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center, in Merritt Island, Florida, US, November 6, 202 (REUTERS)
Off
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the American military carried out a new round of "minor strikes" on Iran's Qeshm Island, which he claimed "knocked out" Iranian air defence systems.
Iranian state media reported that two blasts were heard in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the contested waterway which has been disrupted since the US launched its assault on Iran in February.
The Iranian army said in comments carried by state broadcaster IRIB that their air defences downed a US drone over the island.
But Trump told reporters shortly after that the attacks "knocked out" the air defence systems "in about 15 minutes, maybe five".
Responding to reports of the explosions, US Central Command (Centcom) said that the situation is "relatively calm".
In a post on X late on Friday, it said that the US is “offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
This comes after the US military reported that it had conducted what it described as "defensive strikes" on Monday.
The latest round of strikes is the first since Trump's Republican Party suffered a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections- a loss which was fuelled in part by Trump's war on Iran and subsequent rocketing of energy prices.
Since then, Trump's messaging has been erratic- oscillating between threats to "destroy" Iran and claims that the war is close to being concluded.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory
Thousands of tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded by heavy rains overnight, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation.
Scarce aid entering the territory has left tens of thousands of Palestinians in the war-torn enclave exposed to the elements for a fourth winter in a row- with no fuel and nothing but makeshift tents and shelters for protection.
Red Cross spokesperon Amani Al Naouq told Al Jazeera that she has seen footage of “entire families, entire camps” inundated with water and scrambling to drain their tents and protect their belongings and lives.
In October, Director General for the International Organization for Migration Amy Pope warned that nearly all of Gaza's population require shelter assistance, with the combined supply pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners covering barely 17 per cent of identified winter needs.
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said. "Shelter materials must enter quickly, predictably and at the scale required."
Israel has continued to tightly restrict the entry of aid into the territory, with shelter items- including tent poles, construction materials and mobile homes- almost completely barred as the Israeli authorities consider them "dual use" items.
IOM said that around 8,600 IOM emergency shelter kits are waiting outside Gaza, but continue to be turned away from crossing points by the Israeli authorities.
This has forced humanitarian workers to repurpose salvaged materials to construct makeshift shelters, as storms turbochared by the strengthening El Niño phenomenon batter the territory.

data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Mansour al-Sakni, 33, watched helplessly as rainwater flooded the makeshift shelter on the roof of a building in Gaza City's al-Tuffah neighbourhood, where he lives with his wife and four children.
The family had replaced their old tarpaulins with new ones just two weeks ago. Sakni had sold two water barrels so they could buy new sheets to keep them dry and sheltered.
But when the first winter storm swept across the Gaza Strip, the canopy offered little protection.
“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water. The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too,” Sakni told Middle East Eye.
“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room.”

data.author: Mohamad Elmasry

Submitted by

Washington's support for its ally has become an electoral liability, but ending the annual funding package could pave the way for deeper military cooperation
A Democratic campaign sign showing a mugshot of US President Donald Trump lies on the ground outside a polling station in Indianapolis during the midterm election, on 3 November (USA Today Network via Reuters)
Off
There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel.
Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls.
For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance.
Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities.
An August Marquette Law School poll, for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much.
Appearing on Fox & Friends that morning, Trump asked why Republicans should "suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed", a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, who hours later would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Funding for Israel, Trump said, had become "a bad talking point" for Republicans.
The admission was remarkable, and it demonstrated, perhaps more clearly than anything else, the extent to which a mainstay of American foreign policy has turned into an electoral liability.

data.title: Middle East Eye: IRGC spokesman announces lifting of restrictions on Iranian missiles
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
IRGC spokesman announces lifting of restrictions on Iranian missiles
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards has said that it has lifted restrictions on the range of Iran's missiles.
IRGC spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi reportedly made the comments at a press conference on Saturday, in response to question regarding the country's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei's warning to the US against further attacks on the country.
Khamenei had previously said during a meeting with senior military commanders, that any renewed US or Israeli attck would be met with "with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response".
The leader also reportedly ordered an update of Iran's military target database.
According to Tasnim news agency, Mohebbi was asked on Saturday whether Khamenei's comments meant that limits on the range of Iranian missiles had been removed. He responded : "This restriction has been lifted for us".
“Our duty is to show our capabilities on the battlefield,” he added.

data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Syria denies plans to send troops to Yemen, says military cooperation with Saudi Arabia could expand
Syria has no plans to send military forces to Yemen, a Syrian diplomatic source told state news agency SANA, dismissing reports of a possible deployment as baseless.
The source was outlining the scope of military cooperation with Saudi Arabia, which currently focuses on training Syrian forces, building their capabilities and exchanging military expertise.
Coordination visits by Saudi officials to Syria are set to begin next month, with the cooperation potentially developing into a mutual defence agreement or Syria joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, depending on the shared interests of both countries, the person added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Palestinian Minister of Health warns of outbreak of disease in storm-battered Gaza
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Palestinian Minister of Health warns of outbreak of disease in storm-battered Gaza
Palestinian Health Minister Majed Abu Ramadan has warned of the risk of the outbreak of disease in Gaza as tens of thousands of displaced people have faced flooding while sheltering in makeshift tents.
Israeli restrictions have meant scarce aid- and in particular, shelter materials- is entering the strip, leaving almost all of Gaza's population exposed to the elements and health risks amid rapidly deteriorating sanitation conditions.
Abu Ramdan emphasised that the razing of infrastructure by Israel as part of its onslaught on Gaza has amplified the health risks. Overcrowded displacement camps and the cold and damp conditions inside damaged tents could expose children, infants and elderly people to an elevated risk of respiratory infections.
Meanwhile, lack of clean water, busted sewage systems, and mounting waste pose the risk of water and food contamination, as well as the spread of rodents and insects.
Abu Ramadan also emphasised that widespread malnutrition, particularly among children and pregnant women, means their bodies will be less able to fight off infections.
"What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis, but an escalating threat to public health and people's lives that requires immediate international action commensurate with the scale of the catastrophe," Abu Ramadan said.
